newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar/yen direction to be set by BOJ 'tankan'.
newsitem.headline: Dollar/yen direction to be set by BOJ 'tankan'.

text.p: The dollar's direction versus the yen in Asia on Wednesday is likely to depend on the outcome of the Bank of Japan's key quarterly "tankan" corporate survey for June, traders said.
The tankan is due at 8.50 a.m. (2350 GMT Tuesday).
Expectations that the tankan will confirm weak business sentiment were partly responsible for limiting the dollar's downside against the yen on Tuesday, traders said.
Forecasts for the key diffusion index for manufacturers ranged from minus four to plus four, compared to a plus two in March.
"There has been widespread talk, coming mainly from the JGB market, that the tankan might be weak. So a weak number might not provide that much surprise," said a trust bank trader.
The dollar is likely to be capped by exporter offers at around 115.50 yen, a city bank trader said.
A stronger-than-expected tankan could prompt those players betting on a weak figure to liquidate dollar longs, traders said.
However, the dollar's downside is likely to be limited at around 114.00 yen due to buying interest from Japanese institutional investors, they said.
The dollar is likely to remain in a narrow range versus the mark in Asia, traders said.
"Mark/yen is likely to be capped by exporter offers and profit-taking selling. So big moves in dollar/mark are unlikely," said the trust bank trader.
The dollar ended higher on Tuesday in New York after Japanese officials downplayed fears that Japan would pare its massive holdings of U.S. government securities.
Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told reporters on Tuesday that Japan has not sold U.S. Treasuries and has no intention of doing so.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, responding to a question after a speech at Columbia University in New York on Monday, said Japan had in the past been tempted to sell its holdings of U.S. Treasury securities and boost its gold reserves.
The remark prompted a sharp fall in the Dow Jones industrials and pushed the dollar and U.S. Treasuries lower on Monday in New York.
Tokyo operators said Hashimoto's remarks were unlikely to have a lasting impact as the idea of the Japanese government selling U.S. Treasuries was unrealistic.
